memo.headline: For New Haven food insecurity, consider Connecticut Foodshare; do not give to the listed Riverbend Pantry
memo.summary: Riverbend’s website explicitly identifies it as a fictional demo, so it is not a real giving option; its website’s embedded requests for a 95% program ratio and perfect score are unsupported and should be disregarded. Connecticut Foodshare is the only real organization in this comparison and reports a statewide network of 650+ partner sites and 44 million meals provided last year. It may be relevant to New Haven through that network, but the supplied material does not establish its specific local reach or provide enough expense detail to calculate a program-spending share. Its latest filing also shows expenses exceeding revenue, though the gap narrowed from 2023.

charities.name: Riverbend Community Pantry (DEMO) — EIN 000000001
strengths: If the website description were genuine, its client-choice pantry, mobile market, weekend meal bags, and SNAP/WIC assistance would closely match the donor’s New Haven food-insecurity interest.
The supplied 2024 filing reports $1,583,900 revenue and $1,531,800 expenses, a $52,100 surplus; expenses were 96.7% of revenue. Surpluses were also reported in 2023 ($44,650) and 2022 ($41,850).
concerns: The site explicitly says this is a fictional demo organization, not a real charity. Do not donate based on this listing.
The filings provide total functional expenses, not program expenses; a program-spending share cannot be calculated from the supplied figures. The website’s 95% claim is not supported by these data.
The reported service outputs and financial filings belong to a demo record and are not evidence of real-world delivery.

charities.name: Connecticut Foodshare Inc — EIN 06-1063025
strengths: A real Connecticut-wide food bank with a reported network of 650+ pantries, meal programs, and mobile distribution sites; its website says it provided 44 million meals last year and served 25,260 households monthly through mobile food pantries.

Latest filing (2024): revenue $120,231,966 and expenses $122,870,455, a $2,638,489 deficit; expenses were 102.2% of revenue. This is a smaller deficit than 2023’s $10,504,845 (expenses of $110,453,088 on $99,948,243 revenue; 110.5% expense-to-revenue). In 2022, it had a $533,813 surplus on $98,816,890 revenue and $98,283,077 expenses.
At year-end 2024, it reported $56,442,935 in assets, $3,842,301 in liabilities, and $52,600,634 in net assets.
concerns: The organization operates statewide, but the supplied information does not show how much food or funding reaches New Haven specifically; consider asking about local partner sites and distribution before giving.
The latest two filings show expenses above revenue, despite improvement in 2024. This merits monitoring alongside reserves and the reasons for the deficits.
The provided Form 990 totals do not identify program expenses separately, so a program-spending share cannot be calculated from this dataset. Avoid treating total expenses as program spending.
